extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, math educators, rubric designers, and evaluators (including AI systems) who need to assess whether a mathematical proof is explanatory
extracted.subtask_description: Designing or applying a rubric to judge whether a mathematical proof is explanatory, taking into account multiple theoretical accounts (Steiner, Lange, Kitcher, counterfactual, cognitive) and the role of audience, context, time, and goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-relative explanatoriness
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatoriness depends on 'for whom' a proof is explanatory (e.g., same-area researcher, cross-area researcher, graduate student, undergraduate, non-mathematician).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rubric must specify the intended audience before judging explanatoriness. Different audiences may reach different verdicts; document which audience is assumed. Example categories to declare: same-area researcher, cross-area researcher, graduate student, undergraduate, non-mathematician.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-relative explanatoriness
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatoriness depends on 'what was previously puzzling'—the background knowledge and the prior question the proof aims to resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the prior puzzlement or the state of knowledge against which explanatoriness is assessed (what was hard to understand before this proof?). Evaluation should state the context explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-relative explanatoriness
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof's explanatory status can change over time as the field develops; something less explanatory now may become more so later (and vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rating explanatoriness, indicate the temporal perspective (e.g., at time of discovery, with current background knowledge). Consider historical shifts in what counts as explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal-relative explanatoriness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a proof is explanatory depends on the goal: to explain why, to verify that a theorem holds, or to show how to prove similar results (heuristic/technique extraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the evaluation goal (explain why, explain that, provide methods/heuristics). A proof may be explanatory for one goal and not for another; score relative to the declared goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner test (characterizing property + deformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Steiner's criterion: a proof is explanatory if it identifies a characterizing property of the theorem and exhibits how variation/deformation of the property tracks changes in the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the characterizing-property + deformation/variation test: does the proof show which feature of the hypotheses is essential by showing how changing non-essential features leaves the conclusion intact? Note that Resnik & Kushner provide counterexamples where Steiner's test is neither necessary nor sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lange test (symmetry, simplicity, modal necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lange-style criteria check whether the proof exploits features such as symmetry, simplicity, or modal necessity appropriate to the type of result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depending on result type, ask whether the proof leverages symmetry, parsimony, or modal considerations that ground necessity. This axis may require tailoring to the mathematical domain and result type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kitcher (unification) test
rubrics_metrics.description: Kitcher's unification criterion: a proof is explanatory if it fits the theorem into a shared argument pattern that unifies various results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proof reveals that the theorem is an instance of a more general pattern or schema that explains multiple phenomena; check for shared techniques or motifs that provide unifying understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual (causal-style asymmetry) test
rubrics_metrics.description: A counterfactual-style test: ask whether the conclusion would fail under counterfactual changes to the proof's key ingredients (testing asymmetry akin to causal explanation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counterfactual reasoning to see if changing the putative explanatory elements would change the theorem; this helps identify explanatory asymmetries. Apply with care in mathematical (non-causal) settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive test (produces understanding in trained readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is explanatory if it produces understanding in trained readers (empirically measurable by agreement among mathematicians/readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the target audience reports increased understanding, ability to apply the idea, or insight into why the theorem holds. Empirical studies (Inglis-Aberdein, Sa-Alcock-Inglis-Tanswell, Zeki et al.) find substantial inter-rater agreement, so empirical judgment can be part of the rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-axis scoring (independent criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatoriness should be scored on multiple independent axes (Steiner, Lange, Kitcher, counterfactual, cognitive), since a proof can be explanatory in some senses and not others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark each axis separately rather than collapsing to a single yes/no verdict. Report for each axis whether the proof passes, fails, or partially satisfies it, and provide short justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience specification requirement (operational)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before evaluation, explicitly specify: for whom the proof is evaluated, what that audience already knows, and for what purpose the explanation is judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize the audience/context/purpose triad: choose audience category, list assumed background knowledge, and state the intended explanatory purpose (verification/understanding/method extraction). Without these, explanatory judgments are underspecified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns indicating suspect explanatoriness
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that typically undermine explanatoriness: failing Steiner's deformation test; using unique tricks not part of general patterns; not exploiting the structure of the result; failing to generate understanding in knowledgeable readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these anti-patterns as red flags. Examples: a proof that 'works only for the specific case' (fails deformation), relies on ad hoc trickery rather than generalizable ideas, treats structure as irrelevant, or leaves trained readers unconvinced or unilluminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly report disagreements and limits of objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgement that explanatory judgments can involve deep disagreement; evaluators should report which criteria are contested and recognize some disputes may not be resolvable by further analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating (especially in AI-assisted settings), list criteria with differing judgments, explain the source of disagreement (audience assumption, goal, empirical divergence), and avoid presenting a single definitive label when substantive disagreement remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical corroboration as supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use empirical studies of mathematicians' judgments as evidence bearing on whether there is consensus on explanatory status (studies show substantial but not perfect agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, complement theoretical criteria with survey/experimental data about inter-rater agreement; use such data to calibrate how much weight to give cognitive/consensus-based criteria versus purely theoretical accounts.
